title: Why Are My Periods So Painful?
excerpt: Learn why periods can hurt, which patterns are worth discussing, what clinical assessment may involve, and when pain needs urgent care.

children.text: Periods can hurt because the womb tightens to help shed its lining. Mild cramps may be manageable, but pain that stops you sleeping, moving, studying, working, or caring for yourself deserves medical attention. Severe or worsening pain can also be linked with endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, infection, or another cause.
Why are periods painful?
Period pain is called dysmenorrhoea. The womb (uterus) is a muscle. During a period, it contracts, or tightens, as the lining leaves the body.
Chemicals called prostaglandins help trigger these contractions. Higher prostaglandin activity can be linked with stronger cramps, nausea, loose stools, headaches, or dizziness. The
ACOG painful-period guide
explains that cramps may begin before bleeding and often feel strongest near the start of a period.
Pain is personal, but impact is observable. Missing school, cancelling work, waking through the night, vomiting, or being unable to stand are useful details to share with a clinician.
What are primary and secondary period pain?
Primary dysmenorrhoea means period pain without another pelvic condition found as the cause. It often starts in the teen years after cycles begin to include ovulation.
Secondary dysmenorrhoea means pain linked with another condition. It may begin later, become worse over time, last beyond the first days of bleeding, or occur at other points in the cycle.
Possible causes of secondary pain include:
Endometriosis.
Adenomyosis.
Fibroids.
Pelvic infection.
Ovarian cysts.
Structural differences in the womb or reproductive tract.
A copper intrauterine device in some people.
The pattern offers clues, but it cannot confirm the cause. Read the femio guide to
endometriosis
if pain occurs with sex, bowel movements, urination, or at other times of the month.
Which symptoms are useful to notice?
Track more than a pain score. Note:
Where the pain is: centre, one side, back, hips, or legs.
When it begins and ends.
Whether it is cramping, sharp, burning, aching, or pressure-like.
Whether it occurs outside the period.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dizziness, or headaches.
Pain during sex, urination, or bowel movements.
Heavy bleeding or bleeding between periods.
What the pain stops you doing.
One-sided pain, pain with pregnancy possibility, or a sudden change needs a different level of attention from a familiar cramp pattern.
How do clinicians assess painful periods?

A clinician may ask about your periods, pain, sexual health, pregnancy possibility, medicines, past procedures, and family history. You can ask to pause or decline any examination, and the clinician should explain why it is being offered.

Depending on your age and symptoms, assessment may include an abdominal or pelvic examination, pregnancy testing, infection testing, blood tests, or an ultrasound. Further imaging or referral may be discussed when endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, or another cause is possible.
A normal scan does not make pain unimportant. Some causes of pelvic pain are not visible on a routine ultrasound. The next step should reflect the whole pattern and its effect on life.
How to prepare for an appointment
Start with the effect of pain. Say what it stops you doing. This may be easier than choosing one number on a pain scale.
Bring a short record if you have one. Include period dates, pain days, heavy flow, bowel or bladder symptoms, and pain during sex. Add what you tried and whether it helped.
Questions you may want to ask include:
What causes fit this pattern?
Do I need an examination or scan?
What can each option help with?
Could an option affect pregnancy plans?
When should we review the plan?
You can ask for a chaperone during an examination. You can also ask the clinician to stop at any point. Consent is needed throughout.
If the first plan does not help, return for review. Say what changed and what did not. Ask whether the working explanation still fits.
Pain can have more than one cause. Care may also need more than one approach. You are not wasting anyone's time by asking for the next step.
Bring someone you trust if you want support. They can take notes, ask questions, or help you get home after the visit.
What care can involve
For cramps without an urgent cause, a clinician or pharmacist may discuss:
Anti-inflammatory pain medicines.
Heat, such as a warm bath or covered heat pack.
Gentle movement when it feels possible.
Hormonal medicines that reduce ovulation or bleeding.
Pelvic-health physiotherapy.
Support for sleep and coping with persistent pain.
Specialist review or surgery when another condition is suspected or found.

Do not use a medicine that is unsafe for your age, pregnancy status, allergies, stomach, kidney, liver, heart, or other health needs. Follow the label and ask a pharmacist or clinician when unsure. femio does not provide medicine doses.
The
NHS period-problems guide
recommends seeing a doctor when pain is severe enough to affect daily life.
When to see a doctor

Book an appointment if period pain regularly disrupts daily life, is getting worse, starts after years of easier periods, or continues outside bleeding days. Also seek care for pain during sex, bowel movements, or urination; difficulty becoming pregnant; heavy bleeding; or bleeding between periods.
Tell the clinician what you have tried and whether it helped. Bring period and symptom dates if available. You do not need to prove that the pain is severe enough.
Seek care now:

Get urgent medical help for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, fainting, shoulder-tip pain, severe weakness, fever with worsening pelvic pain, or pain with heavy bleeding. If pregnancy is possible, say so. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Living with period pain day to day

Plan for comfort without accepting severe pain as something you simply have to endure. Keep a covered heat pack, water, and period products accessible if they help. Build in rest where possible, but seek clinical support when pain controls your schedule.
Ask school or work for practical adjustments when needed. Flexible breaks, bathroom access, a place to use heat, or remote work can reduce disruption. You can decide how much health detail to share.
Persistent pain can affect mood, sleep, sex, and relationships. Support for these effects belongs in your care plan too.
How to track painful periods in femio
Log when pain begins, where it occurs, severity, other symptoms, and its effect on daily life. Add period flow and any pain outside the period.
femio can place symptoms beside cycle dates and create a summary. It cannot confirm the cause or decide whether pain is safe to manage at home.
Related guides cover
heavy periods
and
menstrual-cycle basics
. You can also read
how painful periods are assessed
and which
period-pain care options
a clinician may discuss.
Frequently asked questions
Is severe period pain normal?
Pain can be common, but pain that disrupts daily life deserves assessment. “Common” does not mean you must manage it alone.
Can period pain start before bleeding?
Yes. Cramps can begin shortly before a period and continue into the first days of bleeding. Pain that starts much earlier, lasts longer, or occurs throughout the month is useful to report.
Can a normal ultrasound rule out endometriosis?
No. An ultrasound can find some causes of pain, but it may not show all endometriosis. A clinician uses symptoms, examination, imaging, and other steps as needed.

title: What Is PCOS? Signs, Assessment, and Care
excerpt: Understand what PCOS is, the signs it can cause, how clinicians assess it, and the care options they may discuss with you.

children.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a long-term hormone and metabolic condition that can affect periods, ovulation, skin, hair, fertility, and health over time. Signs differ from person to person, and having ovarian cysts is not required. A clinician confirms PCOS by looking at a group of signs and ruling out other possible causes.
What is PCOS?

PCOS affects how the ovaries work and how the body handles some hormones. Androgens are hormones that everyone makes, but higher levels or stronger effects can be linked with increased facial or body hair, acne, scalp hair thinning, and changes in ovulation.

Metabolic health is also part of PCOS. “Metabolic” refers to how the body uses and stores energy. Some people with PCOS have insulin resistance, which means body cells do not respond to insulin as well as expected. Insulin helps move sugar from the blood into cells.
The
World Health Organization
estimates that PCOS affects 10% to 13% of women of reproductive age worldwide. The estimate can differ by population and by the criteria used.

Despite its name, PCOS is not simply a problem of “cysts.” The small follicles sometimes seen on an ultrasound are not the same as harmful ovarian cysts. Some people with PCOS do not have this ultrasound pattern at all.
What signs can PCOS cause?
Possible signs include:
Periods that are irregular, infrequent, or absent.
Difficulty knowing whether or when ovulation occurs.
Increased facial or body hair.
Acne or oily skin.
Thinning hair on the scalp.
Difficulty becoming pregnant.
Heavy, long, or painful periods for some people.
Changes linked with insulin resistance, such as darker, thicker patches of skin.

Not everyone has every sign. Symptoms may also change through adolescence, trying to conceive, pregnancy, and later life. The WHO notes that PCOS can affect emotional well-being as well as physical health.

Many of these signs have other possible causes. For example, irregular periods may occur in the first years after periods start, during perimenopause, with thyroid conditions, with major changes in energy intake or exercise, or because of some medicines. A symptom list cannot confirm PCOS.
How do clinicians assess PCOS?

A clinician will usually ask about your cycle, skin and hair changes, medicines, family history, pregnancy plans, and general health. They may check blood pressure and discuss blood tests. An ultrasound may be useful in some situations, but it is not always needed.
The WHO describes three main features used in assessment:
Signs of higher androgen activity, seen in symptoms or blood results
Irregular or absent periods linked with irregular ovulation
A polycystic pattern on an ovarian ultrasound

In adults, PCOS may be confirmed when at least two features are present after other causes have been excluded. Assessment in teenagers needs extra care because irregular cycles and acne can be part of puberty. A clinician may use age-specific guidance rather than applying adult criteria too early.
An ultrasound result alone is not enough. In the same way, having regular periods does not always rule PCOS out. Your full history matters.
What care can involve
Care is based on the signs that matter to you, your health history, and whether pregnancy is a current goal. There is no single plan for everyone.
A clinician may discuss:
Support for regular bleeding and protection of the uterine lining.
Medicines that can help with acne or increased hair growth.
Metformin in some situations to support metabolic health or ovulation.
Fertility care when pregnancy is a goal.
Support for sleep, mood, body image, or eating concerns.
Checks for blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol when appropriate.

No medicine is right for everyone. Some options are not suitable during pregnancy or when trying to conceive. Do not stop a prescribed medicine or begin a supplement because of an online article; discuss it with the clinician who knows your history.
Food, movement, sleep, and stress support may form part of care for overall health. This should not be reduced to blame or a demand to lose weight.
ACOG
and
WHO
both describe care as individual and linked to the person's goals.
PCOS and health over time

PCOS is linked with a higher chance of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea, and changes in the uterine lining. These are population links, not a forecast of what will happen to you. Your clinician can decide which checks fit your age, history, and symptoms.

Long gaps between periods can matter because the uterine lining may build up for longer. Tell a clinician if periods are very infrequent or have stopped. Do not wait for a fertility concern before asking about cycle health.
PCOS can also affect mood, self-esteem, and quality of life. Hair growth, acne, fertility worries, or weight stigma can be distressing. These concerns deserve the same respect as physical symptoms.
When to see a doctor

Book an appointment if periods are often irregular or absent, if new hair or skin changes concern you, or if you are having difficulty becoming pregnant. Also seek support if symptoms affect mood, eating, sleep, school, work, or relationships.
Bring a list of current medicines and a few months of period dates if you have them. Note acne, hair changes, bleeding, pain, and any family history of PCOS or type 2 diabetes. You can use the
cycle-length calculator
to summarise several logged cycles.

PCOS itself does not usually cause a sudden emergency. Urgent symptoms such as severe sudden pelvic pain, fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing still need prompt medical help because another cause may be present.
Living with PCOS day to day

Choose goals that match your needs. One person may want more predictable bleeding, another may want support with acne, and another may be focused on pregnancy. It is reasonable for priorities to change.

Write down questions before an appointment. Ask what the clinician thinks is causing each symptom, which checks are being suggested, what each care option aims to change, and when progress will be reviewed.
Avoid comparing your body with before-and-after images or strict plans online. PCOS varies widely, and a plan that fits someone else may not fit your health, culture, budget, or goals.
How to track PCOS in femio

Track period start and end dates, flow, symptoms, and short notes. Useful context might include acne changes, unwanted hair growth, scalp hair changes, sleep, mood, or when symptoms affect daily life. You choose what to record.
femio can show cycle estimates as ranges and create a visit summary from your entries. A log can show timing and patterns, but it cannot confirm PCOS or choose clinical care.
Learn more about
how the menstrual cycle works
. Related guides cover
common PCOS signs
how PCOS is assessed
, and
PCOS and fertility
Frequently asked questions
Can you have PCOS without ovarian cysts?
Yes. The name can be misleading. A clinician can confirm PCOS without an ultrasound pattern when other criteria are met and other causes have been excluded.
Can you have regular periods and PCOS?
It is possible. Some people have signs of higher androgen activity or irregular ovulation even when bleeding seems regular. A clinician looks at the whole picture.
Does PCOS always cause fertility problems?
No. PCOS can affect ovulation, but fertility experiences vary. If pregnancy is a goal, a clinician can discuss timing, health checks, and care options that fit your situation.

title: Can PCOS Affect Fertility?
excerpt: Learn how PCOS may affect ovulation and fertility, what to track while trying to conceive, and when a clinical fertility review may help.

children.text: PCOS can make ovulation less regular, which may make conception harder to time. It does not mean pregnancy is impossible. Many people with PCOS become pregnant, with or without added medical support.
The effect is different for each person. A clinician can assess your cycle pattern, goals, health history, and any partner factors.
How can PCOS affect ovulation?
Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. In PCOS, hormone signals may not support regular ovulation in every cycle.

Periods may be far apart, absent for several months, or hard to predict. Some people still ovulate with irregular periods. Others have bleeding without ovulation. A calendar cannot confirm what happened in one cycle.
The
WHO PCOS overview
lists irregular ovulation as a key feature that can affect fertility. Read the main
PCOS guide
for a broader explanation.
Can pregnancy happen with PCOS?

Yes. PCOS does not equal infertility, and it does not give a fixed forecast for one person. Age, how often ovulation occurs, sperm health, the fallopian tubes, other health issues, and time trying all matter.
Irregular periods can make timing less clear. The
trying-to-conceive guide
has steps to plan for pregnancy. It also lists questions for a clinician.
ACOG
explains that irregular ovulation may be a main fertility issue in PCOS. Medical support is available.
What should you track?
A short record can help you. It can also show a clinician the pattern. Track:
Period start and end dates.
Bleeding or spotting between periods.
Cycle lengths and long gaps.
Any ovulation test results, with dates.
Medicines and supplements.
Pregnancy test dates and results.
How long you have been trying.
Relevant health changes or symptoms.
Do not let tracking take over daily life. Choose a level that feels manageable.
Some apps estimate a fertile window from earlier cycles. When cycles vary, the estimate becomes less certain. Read
how the fertile window works
before using an estimate.
These dates support conception planning and awareness. They are estimates, not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.
When should you ask for fertility help?

You can ask for advice at any time you are worried. An early review may be useful if periods are very irregular or absent. It may also help if you know of another fertility concern. Age and health history can make time important.

A fertility review often considers both partners when sperm is part of conception. It may include cycle history, blood tests, and checks guided by the history. The aim is to understand the possible barriers rather than assume PCOS is the only one.
The
2023 international PCOS guideline
supports shared decisions about fertility care and wider health needs.
What care may be discussed?

Care depends on what the assessment finds. A clinician may discuss support for ovulation, checks of the uterus and fallopian tubes when relevant, and a semen analysis when sperm is part of conception.

They may also review health before pregnancy. This can include blood pressure, blood sugar, medicines, sleep, food, movement, smoking, and alcohol. They may discuss vaccines and folic acid too. These talks should be free from blame.
Some fertility medicines require monitoring and are not suitable for self-use. Do not buy or start them without specialist advice. There is no one plan that fits everyone with PCOS.
Still unsure whether PCOS fits your symptoms? Read about
common PCOS signs
. Then see
how PCOS is assessed
Looking after emotional well-being
Trying to conceive can bring stress, grief, or pressure. Irregular cycles may add doubt. Your reaction is valid. You can ask for support before a crisis.

Consider setting limits around tracking, testing, or fertility conversations. Tell a clinician if worry, low mood, sleep problems, or eating concerns affect daily life. Support can be part of fertility care.
Avoid language that blames your body. A difficult month or missed tracking day does not mean you caused the problem.
When to see a doctor

Book an appointment if periods are repeatedly far apart or absent, you have been trying without success, or you want help planning around PCOS. Seek advice before trying if you take medicines that may not be suitable in pregnancy.
Contact a clinician for a positive pregnancy test and pain or bleeding. They can advise what assessment is needed based on your symptoms and history.
Seek care now:

Get urgent medical help for severe one-sided pelvic or abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, severe dizziness, or heavy bleeding when pregnancy is possible. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Frequently asked questions
Does PCOS mean I cannot become pregnant?
No. Many people with PCOS become pregnant. The support needed, if any, varies.
Can regular bleeding prove that I ovulate?
No. It may suggest a pattern, but bleeding dates alone cannot confirm ovulation in every cycle.
Should fertility assessment only focus on PCOS?
No. Other factors can matter, including sperm and the fallopian tubes when relevant.
Are app fertile-window dates exact with PCOS?
No. Irregular cycles make calendar estimates less certain.

sources.title: ASRM: 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS

title: PCOS: Hair, Skin and Mood
excerpt: Extra hair, acne, hair thinning and mood changes can come with PCOS. Learn what to note, how screening works and when to get help now.

children.text: Extra hair on the face or body, acne, oily skin and thinning hair on the scalp are possible signs of PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome). Anxiety and low mood are also linked with PCOS. These changes can affect how you feel about your body and your daily life.
This is health information for learning and planning. It is not medical advice. A screening questionnaire can start a conversation with your clinician. It cannot confirm PCOS or any mood problem.
Seek care now:
If you have thoughts of ending your life or of harming yourself, get help now. Visit the
help page
for support routes. You can also contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Extra hair on the face or body

The World Health Organization (WHO) lists excess hair on the face or body among the signs of PCOS. The medical name is hirsutism. The NHS describes it as thick, dark hair on places such as the face, neck, chest or tummy. Lighter, finer hair is usually not hirsutism.

The NHS says hirsutism is usually linked to higher levels of "male-type" hormones (androgens), or to the body being more sensitive to them. PCOS is the most common cause. Sometimes no cause is found. Less often, it comes from certain medicines or other hormone conditions.

The 2023 international PCOS guideline says a clinician may score hair growth across several body areas. The cut-off used can vary by ethnic background. The guideline also says extra hair on its own is a stronger clue to PCOS in adults than acne or hair thinning on their own.
Hair removal options include shaving, waxing, creams, electrolysis and laser, the NHS says. Your clinician can talk through these, and medicines for extra hair too. See
treatment options to discuss
Acne and oily skin
WHO lists acne and oily skin as possible PCOS signs. The guideline says acne on its own, without extra hair, is a weak clue for PCOS.
Acne has many causes. The NHS lists hormone changes during puberty, periods and pregnancy. It also lists PCOS, some medicines, and skin or hair products that make skin greasy.
The NHS says creams, gels and tablets can help acne. A pharmacist can advise on creams you can buy. Ask your clinician which option suits your skin and health.
Thinning hair on the scalp
WHO also lists female-pattern hair thinning on the scalp as a possible sign. The guideline says hair thinning on its own is a weak clue for PCOS.

Hair loss has other causes too. The NHS lists illness, stress, weight loss, iron deficiency and cancer treatment. Female-pattern hair loss can also run in families. So a clinician may check for other causes.
Note when the thinning started and whether it is getting worse. This helps your visit.
Anxiety, low mood and body image
WHO says people with PCOS may have anxiety, depression, eating disorders and a negative body image. WHO adds that symptoms such as unwanted hair face social stigma in many places.

The guideline says clinicians should screen all adults and teens with PCOS for depression. It says they should screen adults for anxiety too. They should use questionnaires checked for use in your region. A screen is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Share your answers with your clinician.
The guideline says the best gap between repeat screens is not known. One practical approach is a screen at diagnosis, then again based on your clinician's judgement and your life events.
The guideline also says eating disorders should be considered in PCOS, whatever a person's weight. It notes that PCOS features can affect body image.
Support that can help

If depression, anxiety or an eating disorder is found, the guideline says psychological therapy should be offered. It names cognitive behaviour therapy as one option for body image worries and eating problems. The NHS describes it as a talking therapy where a therapist helps you change how you think and act.
The NHS also says talking therapy can help when PCOS symptoms lead to depression or anxiety. You can ask about it at any visit.
You do not have to raise everything at once. Start with the change that worries you most. Your feelings about these changes are valid.
When to see a doctor

Ask for an urgent GP or clinic appointment if new thick, dark hair suddenly starts growing on your face and body. Do the same if your voice is getting deeper or your muscles are getting bigger. The NHS gives this advice. The guideline says changes that start suddenly or get worse quickly need further checks.

Book a visit if acne, hair changes or mood affect your daily life, work or relationships. The NHS uses this same test for when to see a GP about PCOS symptoms. The NHS also advises a GP visit if acne is painful or deep, is leaving scars, or is affecting your mental health.
Book a visit if low mood or worry lasts, or keeps coming back. Book a visit if you have worries about eating or body image.
Questions to ask your clinician
Which hair score or check do you use for me?
Could my acne or hair change have another cause we should check?
Would a mood check fit this visit?
What support is available near me, such as talking therapy?
Which hair or skin option fits my goals?
What femio does and does not do.

femio lets you note hair, skin and mood changes, so your visit is clearer. femio does not confirm PCOS. A screen it offers is a starting point, not a diagnosis. femio is not a crisis service. For urgent help, use the
help page

title: PCOS and Insulin Resistance, Explained
excerpt: What insulin resistance is, why it matters with PCOS, how clinicians check blood sugar, and what metformin is. Explained without any dose.

children.text: Insulin resistance means your body does not respond to insulin as well as it should. Insulin is a hormone that helps sugar (glucose) move from your blood into your cells. The World Health Organization (WHO) says PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is linked with a higher long-term risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
This page explains the idea. It is health information for learning and planning, not medical advice. Only your clinician can say what your own blood tests mean.
Seek care now:

If you take metformin, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department if you have signs of too much acid in the blood (lactic acidosis). The NHS lists being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems and feeling very tired as signs. Do the same for signs of a severe allergic reaction, such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash, or trouble breathing.
What insulin resistance is

The US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) describes insulin resistance as a condition where your body does not respond to insulin the way it should. Insulin is made by the pancreas, an organ in your tummy.

When cells do not respond well, more sugar can stay in the blood. Over time, this can lead to higher blood sugar levels. NIDDK lists PCOS among the conditions that raise the chance of insulin resistance and prediabetes. Prediabetes means blood sugar is higher than usual, but not high enough to be type 2 diabetes.
Insulin resistance is not the same as diabetes. NIDDK says people with insulin resistance and prediabetes usually have no symptoms. That is why blood tests matter more than how you feel.
Why it matters with PCOS

WHO says women with PCOS have a higher risk of other health conditions. These include type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. After a PCOS diagnosis, WHO advises further blood tests. These look for insulin resistance and check overall heart and blood vessel risk.
The NHS lists thick, dark patches of skin on the neck or armpits among possible PCOS symptoms. Tell your clinician about any skin change like this.
How a clinician checks blood sugar

Insulin itself is not usually measured. The 2023 international PCOS guideline says insulin tests that clinics can order have limited value and are not recommended in routine care. NIDDK also says the insulin resistance test is mainly used in research.

Instead, the guideline names the 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) as the most accurate way to check blood sugar in PCOS. MedlinePlus, from the US National Library of Medicine, explains how it works:
You do not eat for at least 8 hours before the test.
A first blood sample is taken.
You drink a sweet liquid that contains a set amount of glucose.
More blood samples are taken over the next few hours.
If an OGTT cannot be done, the guideline says two other tests may be used. These are less accurate:
Fasting glucose
measures blood sugar after you have had nothing but water for at least 8 hours.
HbA1c
shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months.
The guideline says an OGTT should be offered to all women with PCOS who are planning a pregnancy or seeking fertility treatment.
Lifestyle and blood sugar

NIDDK says healthy food and drinks and being active may help reverse insulin resistance and prediabetes. The PCOS guideline says lifestyle support aims to improve metabolic health, such as blood sugar and blood fat levels. It also says healthy habits help even without weight loss. See the
lifestyle and weight guide
What metformin is

Metformin is a prescription-only medicine. The NHS says it is used for type 2 diabetes, for gestational diabetes (diabetes that starts in pregnancy) and for PMOS. The NHS now uses the name PMOS (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome), which it says used to be called PCOS. You may hear both names.

The 2023 guideline says metformin may be considered for some adults with PCOS. Its main use is metabolic health, such as insulin resistance, blood sugar and blood fats. The evidence behind this is limited. For extra hair, the guideline prefers the combined pill over metformin. Your clinician decides with you whether metformin fits your goals.
Like all medicines, metformin can cause side effects. The NHS lists these common ones:
feeling or being sick
diarrhoea
tummy pain
loss of appetite
a change in how things taste

The guideline says stomach side effects are often mild and tend to ease over time. Both the NHS and the guideline say metformin can lower vitamin B12 levels, which can make you tired. Serious side effects are rare. The warning signs are in the box near the top of this page.
Questions to ask your clinician
Do I need a sugar drink test (OGTT) or another blood test?
What would a result change in my plan?
Is metformin an option for my goals, and which side effects matter for me?
Should I have my vitamin B12 checked?
Should I have a check for heart and blood vessel risk?
When should we repeat my blood sugar checks?
When to see a doctor
Book a visit if you have PCOS and have not had any blood sugar checks. If you are planning a pregnancy or fertility treatment, ask about an OGTT.

The NHS lists signs of type 2 diabetes that are worth a GP visit. These include feeling very tired, passing urine more than usual, feeling thirsty all the time, and losing weight without trying. Blurred vision, cuts that heal slowly, and itching around the vagina or repeated thrush are also on the list.
Book a visit if a medicine causes side effects that worry you. Talk to your clinician before you make any change to a prescribed medicine.
What femio does and does not do.

femio can help you keep notes on cycles, skin changes and questions for your visit. femio does not measure insulin, read your blood tests, or choose a medicine. femio does not diagnose PCOS or insulin resistance, and it is not medical advice.

title: PCOS: Food, Movement and Weight, Without the Blame
excerpt: What the 2023 international PCOS guideline says about food, movement, sleep and weight. No single diet is proven best, and weight stigma can cause harm.

children.text: Healthy eating, regular movement and good sleep are part of care for PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome, a hormone condition that can affect periods, skin, hair and fertility). The 2023 international PCOS guideline recommends healthy habits for everyone with PCOS. It does not name one diet as the best. It also says these habits help even when your weight does not change.
femio gives health information for learning and planning. It is not medical advice, and it does not replace your clinician.
What the guideline says about lifestyle
The 2023 guideline calls lifestyle a core part of PCOS care. A lifestyle plan can be exercise alone. It can also mix healthy eating, exercise and support with daily habits.
One aim is better metabolic health. Here, that means things like blood sugar and blood fat levels. Another aim is general health and quality of life.
The guideline is clear on one point. There are benefits to a healthy lifestyle even without weight loss. So a change on the scale is not the only sign that something is working.
The guideline also says your goals should be set with you, not for you. You and your clinician agree on them together.
No single diet is proven best
The guideline found no evidence that one type of diet works better than another for PCOS. Any eating pattern that follows general healthy-eating advice can help your health.

That means you do not need a special "PCOS diet". The food you already eat at home can fit, as long as it follows that general advice. The guideline says changes should suit your food likes and your daily life. It also notes that money, culture and family life can make change harder. These are real limits, not personal failings.
The World Health Organization (WHO) also says healthy eating and physical activity matter for all women with PCOS.
Be careful with strong diet claims online. The guideline asks clinicians to warn about wrong health information and to point to trusted sources.
Movement that fits your life
The guideline found no proof that one type or intensity of exercise is best. Any activity that matches general activity advice has health benefits. Doing some activity is better than doing none.

For adults, general advice is 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity each week. Another option is 75 to 150 minutes of harder activity. Adults are also advised to do muscle-strengthening work on two days that are not back to back. For teens, the advice is at least 60 minutes of activity a day.
Activity is not only sport. The guideline counts walking or cycling to get somewhere, active work and housework. Sitting less also helps.

Support with habits can include setting a small goal, keeping notes and solving problems as they come up. Start at a pace you can keep. Ask your clinician what is safe for you if you have other health conditions.
Sleep and snoring
Sleep matters too. People with PCOS have higher rates of obstructive sleep apnoea. The NHS describes sleep apnoea as breathing that stops and starts while you sleep.

The guideline asks clinicians to check for signs of it. The main sign is snoring, together with waking up unrefreshed, feeling sleepy in the day, or tiredness. A clinician may use a short questionnaire or refer you. Only a formal sleep study can confirm sleep apnoea.
Weight, without blame

Many people with PCOS face weight stigma. Stigma means unfair judgement or blame because of body size. The guideline says many women with PCOS experience weight stigma in healthcare and in other settings. It asks clinicians to be aware of their own weight bias.
WHO notes that symptoms such as weight and unwanted hair face social stigma in many places.

The guideline asks clinicians to offer two options. One is weight-focused care, which aims for weight loss. The other is weight-inclusive care, which does not make weight loss the goal. Your goals decide which approach fits you. The guideline gives one simple example of respectful care: asking your permission before weighing you.
This page sets no weight, calorie or kilogram target. Any weight goal should be a shared decision with your clinician, and only if you want one.
Planning a pregnancy
If you hope to get pregnant, the guideline says healthy habits are worth looking at before pregnancy. This includes activity, sleep and mental health. See
PCOS and fertility
for more on this.
Questions to ask your clinician
Which healthy habits would help my goals most, such as periods, fertility or blood sugar?
Would a dietitian or an exercise plan suit me?
Should I have a sleep check if I snore and feel tired during the day?
Which signs of progress, besides weight, can we track together?
Can we talk about weight only when I say yes?
When to see a doctor

Book a visit if you snore and also wake up unrefreshed or feel tired during the day. The NHS also advises seeing a GP if your breathing stops and starts in your sleep, or you are always tired in the day.

Book a visit if worries about eating, exercise or body image affect your daily life. The guideline says eating disorders should be considered in PCOS whatever a person's weight. If an eating problem is suspected, a qualified professional should assess it in full.
Bring your notes on habits, sleep and questions. Ask what each suggestion aims to change, and when you will review it together.
What femio does and does not do.

femio helps you note cycles, habits and questions, so a visit is clearer. femio does not diagnose PCOS, set food, exercise or weight goals, or choose a treatment. femio is not a substitute for your clinician.

WHO fact sheet: Polycystic ovary syndrome (22 January 2026)
NHS: Sleep apnoea, last reviewed 11 May 2026

title: What Are the Common Signs of PCOS?
excerpt: Learn about common PCOS signs, why they vary, what details may help at an appointment, and when changes need medical care.

children.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, can affect periods, ovulation, skin, hair, and fertility. The signs vary, and not everyone has all of them. Other health issues can cause similar changes, so a symptom list cannot confirm PCOS.
The main
PCOS guide
explains the condition in more detail. This page focuses on what you may notice and what to record.
Changes in periods or ovulation
PCOS can be linked with ovulation that happens less often or not at all in some cycles. Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary.
Possible signs include:
Long gaps between periods.
Fewer periods than expected.
Periods that stop for several months.
Bleeding that is hard to predict.
Heavy bleeding after a long gap.
Some people with PCOS have periods that seem regular. A calendar pattern alone does not confirm or rule out the condition.
Read
menstrual cycle basics
to learn how cycle days are counted. The
WHO PCOS overview
explains that irregular or absent periods are among the possible features.
Skin and hair changes
PCOS may involve higher androgen activity. Androgens are hormones present in all people. Higher levels or stronger effects can change hair and skin.
Possible signs include:
Coarse hair growth on the face, chest, abdomen, or back.
Acne that continues beyond the teenage years or is hard to manage.
Thinning hair on the scalp.
Oily skin.
Hair patterns differ by family and background. Acne and hair changes also have many other causes. What matters is the pattern, timing, and whether it is new or distressing.
Rapid new hair growth, a deepening voice, or other fast body changes need prompt medical assessment because they are less typical of PCOS.
Fertility changes
When ovulation is irregular, it may take longer to become pregnant. This does not mean pregnancy is impossible. Many people with PCOS become pregnant with or without added medical support.
The guide to
PCOS and fertility
explains conception planning, when to ask for help, and why care should fit the individual.
Do not use irregular periods as proof that pregnancy cannot happen. Ovulation may still occur in an unexpected cycle.
Other changes that may occur
Some people with PCOS notice weight gain or find weight changes hard to manage. PCOS can occur at any body size, and body size alone says nothing certain about the condition.

PCOS is also linked with a higher chance of some long-term health concerns, including changes in blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol, sleep, and emotional well-being. These concerns usually have no clear symptoms at first. A clinician may discuss checks based on your history and current guidance.

Dark, thickened skin patches can be linked with insulin resistance. Insulin resistance means the body does not respond to insulin as well as expected. It can occur with PCOS, but the skin change is not proof by itself.
The
ACOG PCOS guide
describes the range of cycle, hair, skin, and metabolic features clinicians may consider.
What should you track?
Record facts that can help explain the pattern:
Period start and end dates.
Spotting and the heaviest flow days.
Long gaps without bleeding.
New acne or hair changes and when they began.
Medicines and supplements.
Pregnancy goals or pregnancy possibility.
Sleep, mood, and effect on daily life.
Photos may help show a skin or hair change over time if you are comfortable taking them. Store them securely. You never need to share an image you do not want to share.
If bleeding becomes a main concern, use the
heavy-period guide
to prepare useful details.
How are possible PCOS signs assessed?

A clinician will look at the whole picture. They may ask about periods, hair and skin changes, medicines, pregnancy, family history, and health goals. An exam or blood tests may be suggested. Other causes may need to be checked.

An ultrasound is not needed in every situation. Ovaries that look polycystic on a scan do not, by themselves, confirm PCOS. The name can be confusing because the small follicles seen on a scan are not the same as harmful ovarian cysts.
Read
how clinicians assess PCOS
for the criteria and common checks.
When to see a doctor

Book an appointment when periods are repeatedly far apart, stop without a known reason, or become very heavy. Seek advice for new coarse hair growth, severe acne, scalp hair loss, fertility concerns, or changes that affect well-being.
Mention pregnancy possibility, new medicines, and any rapid body changes. Do not wait until every possible sign is present.
Seek care now:

Get urgent medical help for very heavy bleeding with fainting, severe weakness, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain also needs prompt assessment. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Frequently asked questions
Can you have PCOS with regular periods?
Yes. Some people have other features even when bleeding seems regular. A clinician assesses the full pattern.
Does acne mean I have PCOS?
No. Acne has many causes. Timing, other signs, and clinical checks matter.
Do ovarian cysts confirm PCOS?
No. A scan appearance is only one possible part of assessment, and not everyone needs a scan.
Can PCOS occur at any body size?
Yes. Body size alone cannot confirm or rule out PCOS.

title: PCOS: Treatment Options to Discuss With Your Clinician
excerpt: A goal-based guide to PCOS options for periods, fertility, hair and skin, with what the 2023 guideline says and questions to bring to your clinician.

children.text: PCOS care depends on what you want to change. Some people want regular periods. Others want help with acne or extra hair, or want to get pregnant. Your clinician can match options to your goals, your health and your plans for pregnancy.

femio provides health information for learning and planning. Nothing on this page is medical advice or an instruction to start, stop or change a medicine. Every option here is something to discuss with your clinician.
Seek care now:

Get urgent help if you may be pregnant and have a combination of these: sudden, sharp, intense tummy pain; feeling very dizzy or fainting; feeling sick; or looking very pale. These can be signs of an ectopic pregnancy, which is a pregnancy that grows outside the womb. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Options for irregular periods

The 2023 international PCOS guideline says a combined pill could be recommended for adults with PCOS who have irregular periods or extra hair. A combined pill is a hormone pill with two hormones. It is also a form of contraception, so clinicians talk that through as part of the choice. The NHS also lists other hormone options for periods, such as a progestogen-only pill or a hormone coil (IUS).

The World Health Organization (WHO) says combined pills can help regulate the menstrual cycle. They may also reduce acne or excess hair. WHO says treatment choices should be a shared decision between you and your clinician.
Tell your clinician if you are trying to get pregnant. This changes which options make sense.
Options for blood sugar and metabolic health
The guideline says metformin may be considered for some adults with PCOS, mainly for metabolic health. That means things like insulin resistance, blood sugar and blood fats. See the
insulin resistance guide
for what metformin is and its side effects.

Some people ask about weight medicines. The guideline says these may be considered alongside healthy habits. It says effective contraception is needed while taking them, if pregnancy is possible, because there is not enough safety data in pregnancy. Any weight goal is your choice, made with your clinician. See the
lifestyle and weight guide
Options when you want to get pregnant

Ovulation induction means using medicine to help the ovaries release an egg. The guideline describes these steps for people with PCOS who do not release eggs regularly and have no other fertility problem:
Letrozole

is the guideline's first-choice medicine for ovulation induction. The guideline notes that letrozole is still used "off-label" in many countries. This means it is not formally licensed for this use there. Availability depends on where you live.
Clomifene
(also spelled clomiphene) is an older tablet. The guideline prefers letrozole over clomifene. Clomifene may also be combined with metformin.
Metformin
alone could be used in some cases. The guideline prefers clomifene over metformin alone for this goal.
Gonadotrophins
are hormone medicines that help the ovaries release an egg, the NHS says. The guideline sees them as a second step if tablets have not worked.
Keyhole ovarian surgery
is another second step, for some people whose ovaries did not respond to clomifene. The NHS says it uses heat or a laser on part of the ovary, which may help eggs be released.
IVF

(in vitro fertilisation) is a third step if earlier options have not worked. In IVF, eggs are fertilised with sperm in a laboratory. The embryo is then placed in the womb (uterus), the NHS says. The guideline says putting back one embryo at a time lowers the chance of twins or more.
The NHS PCOS page names clomifene for fertility and does not mention letrozole. Guidance differs between countries and changes over time. Ask which guideline your clinic follows.

Before any ovulation medicine, the guideline says pregnancy should be ruled out. It also lists folate, a B vitamin, as part of planning a pregnancy. Some people need a higher amount, so ask your clinician what is right for you. The guideline also says a sugar drink test (OGTT) should be offered when you plan a pregnancy or fertility treatment. See
PCOS and fertility
for more.
Options for extra hair and acne
The guideline says the combined pill can be used for extra hair, and may be preferred over metformin for that goal.

If the pill or hair removal has not helped enough after at least six months, the guideline says anti-androgen medicines may be considered. Anti-androgens block some effects of "male-type" hormones. The NHS names spironolactone as one example. The guideline says anti-androgens are used together with effective contraception if pregnancy is possible.

Laser or light treatment may be considered for extra hair on the face, the guideline says. People with PCOS may need more sessions. The NHS also lists shaving, waxing, hair removal creams and electrolysis.

For acne, the NHS lists prescription creams or gels, and tablets such as antibiotics or the combined pill. A pharmacist can also advise on creams you can buy. Ask which option suits your skin and health.
Supplements and other choices

Inositol is a supplement. The guideline says it may be considered based on your own preferences and values. It has limited harm, but limited benefit for ovulation, extra hair or weight. The guideline cannot yet recommend a specific type or amount.
Do not start a supplement because of an online article. Talk to your clinician first, especially if you take other medicines.
When to see a doctor

If your periods are irregular or missing and you want to get pregnant, you do not need to wait a year. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) says fertility tests should start without delay for irregular cycles or missing periods. See
when to seek fertility help

Consider a clinical review if you have gone 3 months without a period after having regular cycles, or 6 months if your cycles were already irregular. Seek advice sooner if pregnancy is possible or symptoms worry you.
Book a visit if acne, hair changes or mood affect your daily life, work or relationships. The NHS uses this same test for when to see a GP.
Ask for a review if a plan is not helping, if side effects worry you, or if you are trying to get pregnant without success.
Questions to ask your clinician
Which goal should we focus on first?
Which option fits that goal, and why?
Is letrozole an option where I live?
Which options would you suggest if I am not trying to get pregnant?
What side effects should I watch for with each option?
Do I need any tests before we start?
When will we review how it is working?
What femio does and does not do.

femio helps you record cycles, hair and skin changes, and questions for your clinician. femio does not recommend, choose or dose any medicine, and it does not treat PCOS. This page explains options a clinician may discuss. It is not a plan.
