title: Week 40 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
excerpt: Week 40 contains the due date, which is an estimate rather than a deadline. Term runs to 42 weeks, and nothing is late inside it.

children.text: Week 40 contains the due date, and the due date is an estimate rather than a deadline. Term runs from 37 to 42 weeks, which means a birth anywhere in that five-week band is on time. A birth from 37 to 42 weeks is within term, although from 41 weeks your service will discuss induction and extra monitoring.
Your body this week

In a first pregnancy there is usually an antenatal appointment this week: blood pressure, bump measurement, and a urine sample checked for protein. The pre-eclampsia checks continue right to the end because the condition can appear right to the end.
Practice contractions are frequent and should not hurt. Real contractions do: the bump goes tight and painful, then the pain goes as the muscles relax.

The NHS describes labour in three stages — contractions opening the cervix to about 10cm, the birth itself, and the placenta being delivered — and says the first stage can take many hours, and is often shorter for women who have given birth before.
What you may notice
Something like premenstrual heaviness, or a low backache, can be an early sign. Alongside: practice contractions, sleep problems, backache, piles, indigestion, leg cramps, swelling and dizziness.

The call threshold is unchanged: contact the unit when contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every five minutes, and at any time if waters break, if there is bleeding, or if movements change.

Movements matter as much this week as any other. The NHS says plainly that movements should not slow down or stop, and that a change is a reason to contact the maternity unit straight away, at any hour.
Your baby this week
Around week 40, the length given is about 51.2cm from head to heel — pumpkin-sized, in the NHS's comparison. It is a population average and never a measurement of an individual pregnancy.
It is cramped, and movements continue in their usual pattern regardless.
What care usually happens around now

If labour has not started, the conversation moves to what happens next. NHS guidance is that induction is offered if labour has not begun by 41 weeks, and that women who prefer to wait should be offered increased monitoring of their own and their baby's wellbeing, with a further offer if a pregnancy reaches 42 weeks. ACOG describes the same decision being made with a clinician, weighing the individual pregnancy.

There are no proven ways to safely bring on labour at home, and the NHS advises checking with a midwife or doctor before trying anything beyond waiting. What is offered, and when, differs between countries.
This week's tip

Stop counting days past the due date and start counting weeks of term. The due date was calculated from a period date or a scan and it was always an estimate. Reframing the wait as "somewhere in a five-week window" is not a consolation — it is a more accurate description of what a due date is, and it is what makes the last fortnight bearable.
When to see a doctor
Call the maternity unit for contractions lasting 60 seconds every five minutes, for waters breaking, for bleeding, or for any change in movement.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list, and
postpartum recovery in the first six weeks
covers what comes next.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (
help now
). Contact your maternity service straight away if your baby's movements slow down, stop or change. femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Is my baby late?

Not necessarily. Term is 37 to 42 weeks, and a due date is a single estimated point inside a five-week band; if you go past 41 weeks your service will discuss next steps. Most women give birth in the week either side of it.
Can I do anything to bring on labour?
There are no proven safe home methods, and the advice is to ask a midwife or doctor before trying anything.
Week 39
covers waters and shows, and your service will discuss what happens at 41 and 42 weeks.

sources.title: NHS: Week 40 - week-by-week guide to pregnancy
ACOG: When Pregnancy Goes Past Your Due Date

title: Week 5 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
excerpt: Week 5 is when most women find out. Tiredness often arrives first, and the heart and nervous system are taking shape.

children.text: Week 5 is when a great many women find out. A missed period has usually registered by now, and home tests are reliable at this point. Excitement and worry arriving together is ordinary, not a sign that anything is wrong.
Your body this week
There is still nothing to see. What there is, is tiredness — the kind the NHS describes as extreme, and the kind that is hard to explain to anyone who does not know yet.

Hormone levels are climbing steeply, and they are behind most of what you feel. Some women notice light bleeding around this time and assume it is a period arriving late. It can also be implantation bleeding, when the embryo attaches to the lining of the womb.

Worry is common enough to be worth naming. NHS guidance points out that around one in five women feel anxious or stressed during pregnancy, and it advises talking to a midwife or doctor rather than sitting with it. That is not a sign of coping badly.
What you may notice

The NHS lists tiredness, a metallic taste, sore breasts, nausea at any hour, mood swings, new food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, needing to pee more often, a milky white discharge, cramping like period pain, and light spotting.
Food cravings and aversions can start now. Both come from hormones changing how taste and smell work, and neither predicts anything about the pregnancy.
Two things do not belong on a wait-and-see list: heavy bleeding, and pain that is severe or concentrated on one side. Both need to be assessed today.
Your baby this week
Around week 5, an embryo is roughly 2mm long — about the size of a sesame seed, as the NHS illustrates it. These are population figures, and no woman's own pregnancy has to match them.

This is the week the heart begins to form and beat, and the brain and spinal cord are taking shape rapidly. Blood vessels are appearing, and some of them will become the umbilical cord. The placenta is being built and will eventually take over from the yolk sac.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing is routinely scheduled. This is the week to make contact if you have not: the first booking appointment usually falls between weeks 8 and 12 in the UK, and services elsewhere run to different timetables.

If you take medication for an existing condition, guidance is to tell your prescriber that you are pregnant rather than stopping anything on your own. That single conversation is more useful this month than any other.
This week's tip

Book the midwife or GP appointment today rather than after the weekend. Waiting lists exist, the booking appointment takes about an hour, and every screening choice offered later has a window attached to it. Getting into the system early is the one thing this week that changes what is available to you in weeks 11 to 14.
When to see a doctor
Any bleeding should be reported, even if it settles. So should severe pain, one-sided pain, pain at the tip of the shoulder, or feeling faint.
Early pregnancy changes
covers what is ordinary this early, and
pregnancy warning signs
covers what is not.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (
help now
). femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
I bled a little and I am still testing positive. What does that mean?

It needs to be assessed rather than interpreted at home. Light spotting is common and often harmless, and it can also be the first sign of something that needs care today. Contact a midwife, GP or early pregnancy unit.
Should the tiredness be this bad?
For many women it is, and it usually eases in the second trimester.
Week 6
covers the nausea that often arrives next, and
week 4
explains why the counting starts where it does. If tiredness is stopping you functioning, say so at your first appointment.

sources.title: NHS: Week 5 - week-by-week guide to pregnancy

title: Week 6 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
excerpt: Week 6 is when nausea often starts, at any hour of the day. Limb buds and ears are beginning to form.

children.text: Week 6 is when nausea most often turns up, and it rarely keeps to mornings. The name is one of the least accurate in medicine. Meanwhile arms, legs and ears are starting to form, all inside something the size of a pea.
Your body this week
Outwardly, nothing. Inwardly, hormones are running at a level most women feel. Nausea, exhaustion and a sense of smell that has become a liability are the three complaints of this week.

The NHS describes morning sickness as something that can happen at any time of day, though it is often worse on waking. Its practical suggestions are unglamorous and do help some women: a snack by the bed, six small meals rather than three large ones, plenty of fluids, and rest. Some find ginger useful, or ice cubes, or acupressure wristbands.

What matters more than any of those is the line where it stops being ordinary. If you cannot keep food or fluids down, that is a reason to contact a midwife or doctor rather than to endure it. ACOG describes severe, persistent nausea and vomiting in pregnancy as a condition clinicians assess and manage, not a rite of passage.
What you may notice

Alongside nausea and tiredness: a metallic taste, sore breasts, mood swings, headaches, new food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, needing to pee more often, a white milky discharge, cramping like period pain, and bloating.
Many women feel considerably better after the first trimester ends at week 12, which is a long way off when you are in the middle of week 6.
Bleeding, severe pain and one-sided pain are the three things not to wait on. Contact a service today.
Your baby this week

Around week 6, an embryo measures roughly 6mm — the NHS compares it to a pea, and notes some people think it looks like a tadpole with a small tail. The figures are averages drawn from many pregnancies rather than a description of anyone's own.

Arms and legs are appearing as limb buds. There are dents where the ears will be, a bump where the heart is, and another where the head will be. A heartbeat can sometimes be seen on a vaginal ultrasound scan at this stage, though in most systems no scan is offered this early unless there is a specific reason.
What care usually happens around now

Still nothing routine for most women. If you have had fertility treatment, an early scan may be part of your care, and if you have had an ectopic pregnancy before, guidance is usually to be seen early. Both are individual reasons rather than a general schedule, and schedules differ between countries.
This week's tip

Eat something before you get out of bed — literally before your feet touch the floor. Nausea is often worst on an empty stomach after a night's gap, and putting a packet of plain biscuits or crackers on the bedside table the night before is the version of this advice that actually works, because it does not require you to feel well enough to go to the kitchen.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP if you cannot keep fluids down, if you are losing weight, if you feel dizzy on standing, or if you are passing very little urine. Any bleeding should be reported.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (
help now
). femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
My nausea stopped suddenly. Should I worry?
Symptoms come and go, and many women have a good day in the middle of a bad fortnight. It is not something to interpret alone either way — if it worries you, ring your midwife and say so.
Is it normal to feel sick all day?
Yes, and the name misleads people.
Week 7
and
week 5
cover the same stretch. If you cannot keep anything down, that is the point at which to ask for help.

sources.title: NHS: Week 6 - week-by-week guide to pregnancy
ACOG: Morning Sickness - Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

title: Week 7 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
excerpt: Blood volume is already climbing in week 7, which explains the thirst and the dizziness. Brain and spinal cord are growing fast.

children.text: By week 7 there is noticeably more blood moving around your body than there was seven weeks ago. That is behind a lot of the thirst, the warmth and the head-rush on standing. Nothing is visible yet, and most women are still deciding who to tell.
Your body this week

Blood volume rises through pregnancy, and the NHS puts the eventual increase at up to 50%. The extra blood supplies the womb with the oxygen and nutrients a pregnancy needs, and the immediate effect on you is thirst.

The NHS suggests aiming for around eight medium glasses of fluid a day — water, milk, fruit juice or fruit tea all count. Feeling hot, sweaty or lightheaded is common at this stage and usually settles with sitting down.

The womb is around the size of a lemon this week. In a first pregnancy most women do not look pregnant until about week 12; those who have been pregnant before often show earlier because the muscles have stretched before.
What you may notice

Sickness, tiredness and mood swings are the trio most women name. Add a metallic taste, sore breasts, headaches, a heightened sense of smell, a white milky discharge, cramping, bloating, and skin changes such as darker patches on the face.

One symptom deserves separating out even though it sounds minor. Itching all over, particularly if it is worse at night, is something the NHS says to report rather than treat with moisturiser and hope. Tell a midwife or doctor.

Anything that feels strange to you is worth raising, even if it is not on a list. Most of it turns out to be ordinary, and the point of asking is that neither you nor an app is the right thing to be deciding with.
Your baby this week

Around week 7, an embryo measures about 10mm from head to bottom — roughly grape-sized, as the NHS puts it. Averages are all these numbers are, and a scan measuring differently is not a verdict on anything.

The brain grows faster than the rest of the body at this stage, so the forehead is large. There are dimples where the nose and ears will be, eyelids are beginning to form, and the limb buds are laying down cartilage that will become bones.
What care usually happens around now
Most women are waiting for the booking appointment, which usually falls between weeks 8 and 12 in the UK and takes about an hour.
What happens at the first pregnancy appointment
covers what is asked and offered.

Legally, in the UK, an employer does not have to be told until the 15th week before the baby is due. Telling them earlier unlocks paid time off for antenatal appointments and a workplace risk assessment. Employment rules are national, so check what applies where you live.
This week's tip

Fill a bottle in the morning and finish it by evening. Thirst in early pregnancy is real and mostly unnoticed until you are dizzy, and the difference between "I should drink more" and a container you can see the level in is the difference between intending and doing.
When to see a doctor
Report any bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, itching all over, or dizziness that does not settle when you sit.
Pregnancy warning signs
lists the rest.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (
help now
). femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Do I have to tell my employer yet?
Not usually this early. In the UK the deadline is the 15th week before the baby is due, and telling them sooner brings maternity rights forward, including paid antenatal appointments.
Why am I dizzy when I stand up?
Blood volume and blood pressure both change in pregnancy.
Week 8
covers more of the same stretch, and
week 6
covers the sickness. Dizziness that comes with a headache, vision changes or fainting needs care today.

sources.title: NHS: Week 7 - week-by-week guide to pregnancy

title: Week 8 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
excerpt: Week 8 usually opens the booking appointment window, and it is often the week mood swings become the loudest symptom.

children.text: Week 8 usually opens the window for the booking appointment, the longest antenatal appointment most women have. It is also, for many, the week mood becomes the loudest symptom rather than sickness. Both are worth planning for.
Your body this week
You may be bloated and your breasts slightly swollen, but it will probably be several more weeks before you look pregnant.

The placenta is preparing to take over the work of feeding the pregnancy and removing waste. The NHS describes it as sprouting small branches that anchor it to the wall of the womb. That handover is gradual and finishes early in the second trimester.

Feeling anxious or low is common enough that NHS antenatal care asks about it directly. The advice is to say so — to a midwife, to a GP, to someone — rather than to wait and see whether it lifts. There is no threshold you have to reach before it is worth mentioning.
What you may notice
Tiredness, sickness and needing to pee more often as the growing womb presses on the bladder. If that is wrecking your sleep, the NHS suggests drinking plenty during the day and less in the evening.

The rest of the list is familiar by now: a metallic taste, sore breasts, headaches, mood swings, food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, a milky white discharge, cramping, darker patches of skin, and bloating.
Bleeding, severe pain or one-sided pain still belong to today rather than to the next appointment.
Your baby this week

Around week 8, the measurement given is roughly 16mm from head to bottom — about raspberry-sized in the NHS's illustration, and it grows quickly over the following weeks. Population averages, not a description of any one pregnancy.
The head has started to uncurl. Arms are lengthening faster than legs, because the upper body grows first. Later in the first trimester the embryo starts to be called a foetus.
What care usually happens around now

The booking appointment usually happens between weeks 8 and 12 in the UK, takes about an hour, and covers medical history, blood pressure, a urine sample, and blood tests. Screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis is offered, as are screening choices to discuss for later in pregnancy.

A dating scan is offered somewhere between weeks 8 and 14. NICHD describes a similar first-visit pattern in the US, with the schedule set by the clinician rather than a national timetable — so the shape is shared even when the dates are not.
This week's tip

Write your questions down before the booking appointment and take the list in with you. An hour sounds long and disappears fast, and the questions people forget are always the ones they were embarrassed to ask. If a previous pregnancy ended in loss, put that at the top of the list — it changes the care that is offered.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP for any bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, an inability to keep fluids down, or a fever. If you feel unable to cope, say that too.
What happens at the first pregnancy appointment
explains the visit itself.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (
help now
). femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
What actually happens at a booking appointment?
Medical history, blood pressure, urine, blood tests, and a conversation about screening choices and where you might give birth.
Pregnancy warning signs
is worth reading before you go, so you know what to ask about.
I am crying at everything. Is that hormones?
Mood changes are extremely common in the first trimester, and that does not make them trivial.
Week 9
is the week hormone levels usually peak. Tell your midwife how you are feeling — it is a routine question, not a difficult one.

sources.title: NHS: Week 8 - week-by-week guide to pregnancy
NHS: Your antenatal care and appointments
NICHD: What happens during prenatal visits?

title: Week 9 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
excerpt: Week 9 is when pregnancy hormone levels usually peak, which is why it is often the hardest week of the first trimester.

children.text: Week 9 is, for a lot of women, the low point. Pregnancy hormone levels peak around now, and everything they cause peaks with them. It does get better, and knowing that is most of what week 9 has to offer.
Your body this week

Human chorionic gonadotrophin rose steeply in the first weeks, and the NHS puts its peak at around week 9. Oestrogen and progesterone are high too, and together they are increasing the blood supply to the womb.

Breasts are bigger and the waist may be thickening a little, though nothing looks obviously pregnant yet. Some women describe this stretch as an emotional rollercoaster, which is a description rather than a diagnosis, and it is one the NHS repeats because it is so widely reported.
Rest is the only intervention on offer for most of it, and accepting help is worth more this week than at any other point in the first trimester.
What you may notice

Extreme tiredness, sickness, mood swings, a metallic taste, sore breasts, headaches, food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, a white milky discharge, light spotting, cramping, darker skin patches, and bloating.

Eating little and often keeps blood sugar steadier, which for some women reduces nausea. The NHS suggests simple things — a boiled egg with toast, hummus with carrot sticks, pitta with grated cheese — because complicated food is exactly what nobody manages in week 9.
If you cannot keep fluids down, contact a midwife or doctor. That is the line, and it is not a high one.
Your baby this week
Around week 9, the length quoted is about 22mm from head to bottom, which the NHS compares to a strawberry. It is a population figure and nothing about your own scan has to match it.

The face is more recognisable, with eyes now covered by eyelids, a mouth and a tongue with early taste buds. Hands and feet are forming, though fingers and toes are still only grooves. The heart, brain, lungs, kidneys and gut are all developing, and bones are beginning to form.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing routine, unless your booking appointment falls this week. Screening choices for later in pregnancy are usually discussed at that visit, and the dating scan follows somewhere between weeks 8 and 14 in the UK. Timetables vary between countries.
This week's tip

Put three snacks you can eat without cooking somewhere you will see them — the desk, the bag, the bedside. Week 9 is not the week to plan meals. It is the week to remove every step between being hungry and eating, because an empty stomach makes the nausea worse and the tiredness longer.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP if you cannot keep fluids down, if you are losing weight, if you are passing very little urine, or if you feel faint on standing. Any bleeding should be reported.
Pregnancy warning signs
covers the full set.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (
help now
). femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
When will I stop feeling like this?
Many women improve after the first trimester ends at week 12, though some feel better earlier and some later.
Week 10
and
week 8
sit either side of the peak.
Is being this tired normal?

Extreme tiredness is one of the most reported first-trimester symptoms. It is still worth mentioning at your next appointment, because tiredness has causes other than pregnancy and a blood test is easy.
